html:
The last eruption of Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, from 16 December 1707 to 24 February 1708. It is named after the Hōei era.

It came 49 days after the Hōei earthquake, one of the largest in Japan's history, which with its tsunami had killed thousands along the Pacific coast. The eruption opened a new crater on Fuji's southeast flank, still visible today. Little lava flowed, but huge amounts of ash and cinder fell to the east. Villages near the mountain were buried, and ash fell on Edo, about 100 km away, so thickly that people lit lamps by day.

Farms in the Sagami region were ruined for years. Ash washed into rivers raised their beds and caused floods for decades. The shogunate taxed the whole country to pay for relief, though much of the money was spent elsewhere. The eruption is now used as the model for planning what a new Fuji eruption would do to Tokyo.
sum: The last eruption of Mount Fuji, Japan's highest mountain, from 16 December 1707 to 24 February 1708. It is named after the Hōei era.
